chief_complaint: intractable nausea and vomiting of pregnancy with 10-pound weight loss, ketonuria, and electrolyte imbalance
hpi_details: 26F G1P0 at 9 weeks gestation presenting with persistent vomiting >8 times daily, inability to tolerate oral fluids, 6% weight loss, and 3+ ketones in urine requiring hospitalization for IV crystalloid rehydration, thiamine supplementation, and IV Ondansetron/Promethazine.
ideas: She thinks she caught a severe stomach bug or ate spoiled food on top of her pregnancy nausea.
concerns: She is worried that being unable to keep down water or prenatal vitamins will cause a miscarriage or harm the baby's development.
expectations: She hopes to receive IV fluids and prescription anti-nausea medicine so she can finally keep a meal down.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Hyperemesis Gravidarum Refractory Dehydration, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: intractable nausea and vomiting of pregnancy with 10-pound weight loss, ketonuria, and electrolyte imbalance

Key HPI features: 26F G1P0 at 9 weeks gestation presenting with persistent vomiting >8 times daily, inability to tolerate oral fluids, 6% weight loss, and 3+ ketones in urine requiring hospitalization for IV crystalloid rehydration, thiamine supplementation, and IV Ondansetron/Promethazine.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Hyperemesis Gravidarum Refractory Dehydration.
Current medications: Labetalol 100 mg twice daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Normal nausea of pregnancy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Weight loss >5%.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Hyperemesis Gravidarum Refractory Dehydration
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: 26F G1P0 at 9 weeks with persistent vomiting >8 times/day, 6% weight loss, and ketonuria.

must_ask.objective: Quantify vomiting frequency and fluid intake
must_ask.say: How many times a day are you vomiting, and can you keep down any fluids?
How much weight have you lost since this started?
Have you felt dizzy, or noticed you're urinating less?
Has anyone mentioned your uterus seems larger than expected, or have you had unusual bleeding?

must_ask.objective: Explain the IV rehydration and thiamine plan
must_ask.say: We'll give you IV fluids with thiamine and anti-nausea medication to help you feel better.

history.answer: I am nine weeks pregnant, and I haven't been able to stop vomiting for the past several days.
The morning sickness started mildly around week six, but over the last four days it has gotten much worse and completely unrelenting.
I throw up more than eight times every day, immediately after trying to eat or drink anything and even on an empty stomach.
It is mostly clear foamy fluid and bitter yellowish-green bile, with no blood or foul odor.
I throw up constantly throughout the day and first thing in the morning, but it does not shoot out forcefully across the room.
My upper stomach and chest feel sore from gagging and dry-heaving so much, but I do not have sharp abdominal cramps.
I have still been passing gas, but I haven't had a bowel movement in three days and definitely do not have diarrhea.
I haven't had any fever or chills, and my husband ate all the same meals as me and feels completely fine.
I feel very dizzy and lightheaded when I try to stand, but I do not have a headache, stiff neck, blurry vision, or confusion.
No, I have not bumped my head or suffered any head trauma.
I cannot keep even small sips of water down, my mouth is completely parched, and I only peed once today and it was dark amber.
My mouth feels very dry, but I never had excessive thirst or frequent urination before this, and I don't have diabetes.
I don't have chest pain or shortness of breath, just extreme exhaustion and weakness.
I haven't started any new prescriptions, and I have never touched alcohol, cigarettes, cannabis, or illicit drugs.
I have lost ten pounds since finding out I was pregnant, which is about six percent of my starting weight.
No, I never induce vomiting myself; I desperately want to keep food down for the pregnancy.
I have had no vaginal bleeding, brownish spotting, or passage of any grape-like tissue.
I haven't experienced hand tremors, heat intolerance, or palpitations.
I tried eating plain crackers, toast, and ginger tea, but nothing stays down at all.

I thought I caught a terrible stomach flu or ate something bad that made my morning sickness unbearable. I'm terrified that starving like this means my baby isn't getting any nutrients and might not survive.
I was diagnosed with chronic high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol two years ago.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take labetalol 100 milligrams twice a day for my blood pressure, but I stopped taking my prenatal vitamins because they made me gag.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I do not drink any alcohol, and I stopped having occasional drinks as soon as we started trying to conceive.
I work as an accountant at an office, and I live in an apartment with my husband.
My mother had severe morning sickness during her pregnancies, and my father has hypertension, but there is no family history of GI disorders.
This is my very first pregnancy, my last period was exactly nine weeks ago, and my menstrual cycles were always regular every 28 days.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg, heart rate is 106 beats/min, respiratory rate is 18 breaths/min, body temperature is 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Blood pressure falls to 94/58 mmHg and heart rate increases to 124 beats/min upon standing, demonstrating orthostatic hypotension.
Oral mucosa and tongue are dry with cracked lips; pharynx is clear without erythema or exudate.
Skin turgor is decreased with noticeable tenting, and capillary refill time is delayed at 3 seconds.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended without visible peristalsis or surgical scars.
Bowel sounds are hypoactive across all four quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Mild diffuse epigastric tenderness is present on palpation without involuntary guarding or muscular rigidity.
No rebound tenderness is elicited in any abdominal quadrant.
Patient is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, though visibly exhausted and lethargic.
Neck is supple with full passive range of motion, and Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Sclerae are anicteric, pupils are equal and briskly reactive, and extraocular movements are full without nystagmus.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and without palpable nodules, goiter, or bruits.
External genitalia are normal, cervical os is closed without bleeding or discharge, and adnexa are non-tender.
